newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada budget cuts funds for international aid.
newsitem.headline: Canada budget cuts funds for international aid.

text.p: The Canadian government will spend almost 30 percent less this year on international assistance than it did five years ago.

The budget of the Canadian International Development Agency (CIDA), which oversees Canada's foreign aid programmes, has been slashed from C$3.12 billion ($2.3 billion) in 1991-92 to C$2.22 billion ($1.63 billion) this year, according to budget documents obtained by Reuters.

Don Boudria, Canada's minister of international cooperation, on Wednesday commemorated the 50th anniversary of the founding of UNICEF, the U.N. Children's Fund by announcing a decision to spend C$7 million ($5.1 million) to fund special education programmes for African girls in Malawi, Zambia and Zimbabwe.

"It is within our power to reduce the number that will be forced into child labour -- by fighting poverty, by providing access to basic education, by helping countries to improve and enforce their labour and children's legislation," Boudria said.
But the C$7-million ($5.1 million) new funding pledge pales in comparison to the C$900 million ($660 million) cut in the department's budget since 1991.

"The cuts have been devastating," said Kathleen Ruff, a spokesperson for the Canadian Anti-Slavery Group. "It is shameful how the government has backtracked on its commitment to fighting poverty in the Third World."

More than 250 million children aged between 5 and 14 are working in conditions hazardous to their health, according to UNICEF. It contends that industrialised countries, including Canada, face a growing child labour problem.
Nigel Fisher, the organisation's director of emergency programmes, said the problem may be worsening as Canada attempts to bring its budget deficit under control.
When investment in social services, health care and welfare declines, poor families often respond by taking their children out of school and making them work, Fisher noted.
Boudria conceded that child labour remains a problem in Canada. "Even today, not a major western city is without its under-age workers, street kids and teenage prostitutes," Boudria said.
UNICEF officials are pushing Canada and other Western nations to pass tougher legislation punishing those who exploit child labour.

Extending extraterritoriality -- the ability to charge Canadians with crimes committed against children abroad -- is a good starting point, Fisher said. "It's too easy to say we can't do anything about it because of a difficult economic situation."
